paras: The Benson gambling den expulsion was an 1881 incident in which the citizens of Benson, Arizona, burned the furniture of a gambling den and ordered its occupants to leave by the first train or be lynched, after a deputy sheriff was shot. The episode was known mainly through a one-sentence wire item that ran in Michigan, Wisconsin and Texas papers in September 1881, and none of the reports gave the race of anyone involved.

According to the wire item, the shooting of a deputy sheriff at Benson "caused the citizens to burn the furniture of a gambling den and order the whole party to leave by first train or be lynched." The item named neither the deputy nor the person who shot him nor any member of the gambling party, and it did not say whether the deputy survived.

Arizona papers carried two items that may refer to the same trouble. In a Tombstone letter dated August 25, 1881, the Arizona Weekly Citizen's correspondent reported a rumor of the previous evening that Byrnes, known for "the top and bottom game," had been lynched at Benson. The rumor was contradicted when Byrnes arrived in Tombstone that night in the charge of an officer, booked on a charge of assault to murder. Neither Arizona item mentioned the gambling den or the wounded deputy, so their connection to the wire report rests on place, timing and the lynching rumor alone.

On September 24 the Arizona Sentinel, reprinting the Tombstone Nugget, reported that Under Sheriff Woods and Deputy Nagle had taken Ed Byrnes to Benson to answer a complaint of "making threats to kill in that place during the trouble a week or so ago." Justice Mundell held him for the grand jury in $2,000 bonds, and because he could not give bail that evening he was returned to jail. The Sentinel added that Byrnes was one of the "Top and bottom" sharps who had been ordered out of Yuma by the sheriff. No report was found of arrests among the Benson citizens who burned the den, or of an inquest or trial concerning the shooting.

The wire sentence ran without a headline in news-brief columns, appearing on September 1 in the Crawford Avalanche of Grayling, Michigan, and the River Falls Journal of Wisconsin. The Iowa County Democrat of Mineral Point, Wisconsin, printed it on September 2, and the Weekly Democratic Statesman of Austin, Texas, on September 15. The Avalanche placed it under "Crimes and Criminals" among other shootings and murders, and every version stated the lynching threat flatly, without comment.

Closer to the scene, the Citizen's Tombstone correspondent wrote that the false rumor of Byrnes's lynching was "too good to be true." No paper identified the race of the gamblers, the deputy or the townspeople.

bases: Townspeople burned a gambling den's furniture and ordered its occupants out of town under threat of lynching (A1); nothing in the coverage indicates the targets were Black, so the episode may be outside the anti-Black scope.

The den burning and lynching threat rest on one wire sentence reprinted verbatim (A1, A2, A3, A5); two Arizona items report 'trouble' at Benson and a false lynching rumor about a gambler named Byrnes (A4, A6) but do not mention the den or the deputy, so they do not independently corroborate the core event.
